commonMistakes: Saying Git stores diffs instead of snapshots.
Confusing the staging area with the remote repository.
Claiming git pull only downloads changes without merging.
detailedAnswer: Git stores a snapshot of the whole project in each commit, addressed by a content hash, rather than a chain of diffs. The working tree holds your edits, the staging area holds exactly the changes the next commit will contain, and the repository holds committed history. git add moves changes to the staging area, git commit records them, git fetch downloads without touching your files, and git pull fetches and then merges into your current branch. Git is distributed: every clone has the full history, so you can commit and branch offline.
followUps: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
How do you undo the last commit but keep your changes?
question: Explain Git's three areas and how a change moves between them.
shortAnswer: Working tree to staging area with git add, to the repository with git commit; git fetch downloads, git pull fetches and merges.
tips: Draw the three areas and name the command for each move.
Mention that snapshots, not diffs, are what Git stores.
title: Git three areas

commonMistakes: Saying rebase is safe on shared branches because it is cleaner.
Forgetting that rebase changes commit hashes.
Using git push --force instead of --force-with-lease.
detailedAnswer: A branch is a movable pointer to a commit. When both branches have moved since their merge base, a merge creates a merge commit with two parents, preserving the branch structure. A fast-forward merge simply moves a pointer when the target has not moved. Rebase replays your commits onto a new base for a linear history, but it rewrites commit hashes, so it is only safe on a private, unshared branch. Force-pushing a rewritten branch should use --force-with-lease, which refuses to overwrite work pushed since your last fetch. A bad commit on shared main is fixed with a revert commit, not history rewriting.
followUps: When would you choose merge over rebase for a pull request?
How do you resolve a merge conflict in a service class?
question: What is the difference between merge and rebase, and when is each safe to use?
shortAnswer: Merge preserves history with a merge commit; rebase linearises private history but rewrites hashes, so it is only safe on unshared branches.
tips: State the rule first: rebase private branches, merge shared ones.
Give the --force-with-lease detail to show production awareness.
title: Merge vs rebase

commonMistakes: Saying a container is a lightweight virtual machine with its own kernel.
Confusing an image with a container.
Storing important data in the container's writable layer.
detailedAnswer: A virtual machine runs a full guest operating system on virtualised hardware. A container shares the host kernel and is isolated by namespaces, which give it its own view of processes and networking, and cgroups, which limit CPU and memory. That is why containers start in seconds and use far less memory. An image is a read-only layered template, a container is a running instance of an image plus a thin writable layer, and a registry stores images. Containers are ephemeral: data that must survive belongs in a volume or an external service, configuration arrives via environment variables, and a Spring Boot container runs the JVM in the foreground as its main process.
followUps: What happens to data in a container's writable layer when it is removed?
How do two containers on one network reach each other?
question: How is a container different from a virtual machine, and what is the difference between an image and a container?
shortAnswer: Containers share the host kernel with namespace and cgroup isolation; an image is a read-only template, a container is a running instance of it.
tips: Name namespaces and cgroups explicitly; interviewers listen for them.
Connect it to Java: a jar plus a JDK in an image, run identically everywhere.
title: Containers vs virtual machines

commonMistakes: Shipping a single-stage image with Maven and source code.
Copying source before downloading dependencies, destroying the cache.
Putting a secret in ENV or a copied file, believing a later deletion removes it.
Using the shell form of ENTRYPOINT so signals never reach the JVM.
detailedAnswer: Each Dockerfile instruction is a cached layer, so instructions are ordered from rarely changing to frequently changing: dependencies are downloaded in their own layer before source is copied, so code changes reuse the cached dependencies. A multi-stage build compiles the jar in a JDK stage and copies only the jar into a slim JRE stage, so the final image has no build tools or source. The entrypoint uses the exec form so shutdown signals reach the JVM, the container runs as a non-root user, versions are pinned rather than latest, and .dockerignore keeps target and .git out of the build context. Secrets never appear in a Dockerfile or image layer, because layers are immutable and a later deletion does not remove an earlier layer's content.
followUps: A secret reached an image layer and was then deleted. Is it gone?
Why is the exec form of ENTRYPOINT preferred for Java?
question: Design a Dockerfile for a Spring Boot application. Why multi-stage, and how do you keep builds fast and images safe?
shortAnswer: Multi-stage: build the jar in a JDK stage, ship only the jar in a slim JRE stage; cache dependencies before source, pin versions, run non-root, never put secrets in a layer.
tips: Walk the layers in order and explain the cache at each step.
Mention the secret-in-a-layer trap; it is a favourite follow-up.
title: Dockerfile design for Spring Boot

commonMistakes: Saying a Service stores data or balances by itself without endpoints.
Giving a Service a selector that matches no pods.
Using a liveness probe that fails during normal JVM startup.
detailedAnswer: A pod is the smallest schedulable unit, usually one container, and it is ephemeral: it can be killed and replaced at any time with a new IP. A Deployment declares the desired state and manages ReplicaSets, which keep the requested number of pods running and perform rolling updates by replacing pods gradually, waiting for new pods to be ready. A Service gives a stable DNS name and virtual IP routing to the current healthy pods selected by labels, so clients never depend on pod IPs. ClusterIP serves internal traffic, LoadBalancer provisions a cloud load balancer, and Ingress adds HTTP routing by host and path. Liveness probes decide whether a stuck container restarts, readiness probes decide whether a pod gets traffic, and Spring Boot Actuator provides endpoints for both.
followUps: How does a rolling update work, and how do you roll back?
Why must a Kubernetes application be stateless?
question: Explain pods, Deployments, and Services, and how they work together for a Spring Boot service.
shortAnswer: Pods are ephemeral units; Deployments manage ReplicaSets for self-healing rolling updates; Services give stable DNS routing to healthy pods by label.
tips: Use a concrete example: 3 replicas of a Spring Boot container behind a ClusterIP Service.
Mention Actuator probes by their exact paths.
title: Pods, Deployments, Services

commonMistakes: Using continuous delivery and continuous deployment as synonyms.
Rebuilding a different artifact for production.
Deploying without a smoke test or rollback plan.
detailedAnswer: Continuous integration means merging small changes frequently and verifying every merge with automated builds and tests. Continuous delivery means every passing change is packaged and ready to deploy, with a human triggering the release. Continuous deployment releases every passing change automatically. A pipeline runs stages in order — build, test, scan, package, publish, deploy, verify — with failure stopping later stages, and it is defined as code in the repository. The same artifact travels through every environment: CI builds a container image tagged with the commit SHA, pushes it to a registry, and deployment updates the target to that exact image, followed by a smoke test against the health endpoint and a rollback to the previous image if it fails.
followUps: How do you keep a pipeline fast without skipping tests?
What do you do when main goes red?
question: What are CI, continuous delivery, and continuous deployment, and what does a pipeline for a Java service look like?
shortAnswer: CI verifies every merge; delivery makes every passing change releasable; deployment releases automatically. Build once, promote the same artifact, smoke-test every deploy.
tips: Walk a real flow: pull request, merge, image tagged by commit SHA, rolling deploy, smoke test.
Distinguish delivery from deployment in the first sentence.
title: CI/CD pipeline for Java

commonMistakes: Testing mostly through slow end-to-end tests.
Using an in-memory database and finding dialect differences in production.
Retrying a flaky test until it goes green.
Chasing 100 percent coverage with assertion-free tests.
detailedAnswer: The test pyramid has many fast unit tests at the base, a moderate integration layer, and a few end-to-end tests at the top. Unit tests isolate one class with mocked dependencies and run in milliseconds. Integration tests verify components together against real infrastructure, and Testcontainers runs the genuine database in a container for this layer, avoiding the SQL dialect differences of an in-memory substitute. End-to-end tests cover critical journeys only, because they are slow and brittle. CI runs from a clean checkout, so tests must be deterministic and independent; a flaky test is quarantined and its root cause — timing, shared state, or order dependence — is fixed, never retried away. Coverage is a floor and a review aid, not a target, because it measures executed lines, not asserted behaviour.
followUps: Why Testcontainers instead of an in-memory database?
Is 100 percent coverage a good CI gate?
question: How should tests be structured so a CI pipeline gives fast, trustworthy feedback?
shortAnswer: Follow the pyramid: many unit tests, integration tests against real infrastructure via Testcontainers, few end-to-end tests; deterministic tests, flaky ones fixed not retried.
tips: Name the pyramid and give a Java example at each layer.
State the flaky-test rule firmly; interviewers check for it.
title: Testing in CI

commonMistakes: Saying S3 is a filesystem or a database.
Choosing DynamoDB for workloads needing joins and transactions.
Granting wildcard IAM permissions for convenience.
Making an S3 bucket public by default.
detailedAnswer: Under the shared responsibility model, AWS secures the cloud itself while you secure your data, code, configuration, and access. For compute, EC2 gives full control, Lambda runs event-driven functions without servers, ECS and EKS run containers, and Beanstalk trades control for simplicity. S3 is object storage for files, EBS is block storage for one instance, RDS is managed relational databases — the natural fit for Spring Data JPA — DynamoDB is a key-value store for simple high-scale access patterns, and ElastiCache provides caching. Networking uses a VPC split into public subnets for load balancers and private subnets for applications and databases, with security groups as firewalls, and IAM roles with narrow policies implement least privilege.
followUps: When would you choose DynamoDB over RDS?
Why do databases go in private subnets?
question: Which core AWS services would you use for a Java web application, and why?
shortAnswer: EC2 or containers for compute, S3 for files, RDS for relational data, ALB for traffic, IAM roles with least privilege, all inside a VPC with private subnets for apps and data.
tips: Answer by need, not by listing services: compute, storage, database, networking, identity.
Give the trade-off against the nearest alternative for at least one choice.
title: Core AWS services

commonMistakes: Rebuilding a different artifact for production.
Baking database credentials into the image.
Letting Hibernate auto-update the production schema.
Deploying without health checks or a rollback plan.
detailedAnswer: CI builds a container image and pushes it to ECR tagged with the commit SHA. ECS or EKS runs it across availability zones, an Application Load Balancer in public subnets terminates TLS and forwards traffic to healthy containers, and RDS in private subnets provides the database, reachable only from the application's security group. Configuration arrives as environment variables, database credentials are injected from Secrets Manager by the platform, and schema changes run as versioned Flyway or Liquibase migrations, never Hibernate auto-update in production. Updates are rolling by default, with blue-green for fast rollback or canary for limited blast radius, and a deployment is finished only when Actuator health checks and CloudWatch error and latency alarms confirm it, with the previous image retained for instant rollback.
followUps: How does the application get its database password?
When would you choose ECS over EKS, or Beanstalk over both?
question: Walk through deploying a Spring Boot application on AWS from commit to production.
shortAnswer: CI image to ECR, ECS or EKS across zones, ALB in front, RDS in private subnets, secrets from Secrets Manager, migrations via Flyway or Liquibase, rolling update with rollback.
tips: Follow the path in order and name the service at each step.
Stress the same-image rule before any detail.
title: Deploying Java on AWS

commonMistakes: Claiming a container exit means the application crashed, without checking the main process.
Treating CrashLoopBackOff as a Kubernetes bug rather than a symptom.
Checking logs of the current pod only, missing the previous crashed instance.
detailedAnswer: Start with the platform state, then the application output. kubectl get pods shows status and restart counts; a pod in CrashLoopBackOff is starting, failing, and restarting. kubectl describe pod shows events such as image pull failures or failed probes, and kubectl logs --previous shows the last crashed instance's output, where the startup error usually lives. For a Spring Boot container, the common causes are a backgrounded main process that lets the container exit immediately, a missing environment variable, a database connection failure, or a memory limit below what the JVM needs, which kills the pod in a loop. The fix addresses the cause — foreground process, correct configuration, or a realistic limit — rather than repeatedly restarting the pod.
followUps: Why would a container exit immediately after starting?
How do you tell a liveness probe problem from an application crash?
question: A containerised Java service keeps crashing in Kubernetes. How do you debug it?
shortAnswer: Check pod status and restart counts, describe for events, logs --previous for the crashed instance, then fix the cause: process, config, connection, or memory limit.
tips: Give the command sequence in order; it shows real operational experience.
Mention --previous explicitly; it is the detail most candidates miss.
title: Debugging a crashing container

commonMistakes: Picking a strategy by fashion rather than by rollback and blast-radius needs.
Running a canary without metrics or automated rollback.
Forgetting that stateful services cannot roll like stateless ones.
detailedAnswer: A rolling update replaces instances gradually, waiting for new instances to pass health checks, and is the safe default for stateless services on ECS and EKS. Blue-green runs old and new versions side by side and switches the load balancer once the new version is verified, keeping the old version for instant rollback at the cost of double capacity during the switch. Canary shifts a small percentage of traffic to the new version, watches error rates and latency, and increases the share gradually or rolls back, limiting the blast radius of a bad release but requiring good observability and automated rollback to be effective. The choice follows the service's needs: rolling for simplicity, blue-green when rollback speed matters most, canary once metrics can judge a partial rollout, and feature flags can decouple deployment from release in all three.
followUps: How do you decide a canary is healthy enough to promote?
How does this change for a stateful service?
question: Compare rolling, blue-green, and canary deployments. When would you choose each?
shortAnswer: Rolling is the simple default; blue-green gives instant rollback at double capacity; canary limits blast radius but needs strong metrics and automated rollback.
tips: State the trade-off for each in one clause: simplicity, rollback speed, blast radius.
Mention feature flags as a complement, not a fourth strategy.
title: Deployment strategies

commonMistakes: Saying the JVM automatically fits any container limit without verification.
Setting no resource limits and letting one service starve its neighbours.
Using latest tags so rollbacks become meaningless.
detailedAnswer: A containerised JVM needs its heap sized inside the container's memory limit: modern JVMs detect container limits, but the limit, the heap settings, and the application's non-heap memory must be verified together, or the pod is killed for exceeding its limit and restarts in a loop. Resource requests drive scheduler placement and limits cap usage, so both must be set. Readiness probes must allow for JVM startup time, or Kubernetes withholds or restarts pods that are merely slow to start. Images are pinned by version or digest so a rollout deploys exactly the tested image and rollback restores a known image. Configuration and secrets arrive at run time, sessions live in an external store so any replica can serve any request, and logs go to standard output for the platform to collect.
followUps: How do you size a JVM heap inside a container?
Why must a service behind a load balancer be stateless?
question: What makes a Java application a good citizen on a container platform in production?
shortAnswer: Stateless, health-checkable, correctly sized for its container limit, pinned image, run-time configuration, externalised sessions, logs to standard output.
tips: Lead with the JVM memory point; it is the Java-specific insight.
Connect each practice to a failure it prevents.
title: Java services on container platforms
